newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian students hold lively rallies for change.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian students hold lively rallies for change.

text.p: Thousands of Bulgarian students rock, mock and talk in colourful daily rallies to try to drive the ruling Socialists from power and to press for change in a country on the brink of economic collapse.
From their sombre "march of the dead" to a "Mr and Miss Protest" contest, the students have kept up a spirit of gaiety and non-violence while challenging Bulgaria's ex-communist rulers.
The students are in contact with their counterparts in Belgrade, the Serbian capital, and have exchanged ideas for keeping the demonstrations enthusiastic and entertaining.

"There are a lot of common things between our protest and the rallies of the Serbian students as we are both young with fresh ideas, enthusiasm and a firm commitment to change," said Borislav Borislavov, a student leader from Sofia University.
Serbian protesters have campaigned with festive rallies for 10 weeks to challenge President Slobodan Milosevic and protest against alleged election fraud.
Bulgarian students with towels and bottles of water will hold a "washed hands march" on Tuesday to mock the Socialists' "clean hands" initiative to stop rampant corruption.
Later this week they plan a torch rally and a spoof "Mr and Miss Protest" contest.

Earlier they marched with their faces painted white to symbolise the death of the Socialists, and staged a mock funeral for the ruling party, depositing a flag-draped coffin at the mausoleum of former communist hero Georgi Dimitrov.
The students' main concern is Bulgaria's economic crisis, which has left the lev in freefall and inflation at 300 percent annually and rising rapidly towards hyperinflation.
"We are not bound to any political party and our protests are aimed at bringing change to this country," said Borislavov.

"Some people think we are just having fun in the streets. The truth is we are following the political situation closely and we will step up our protests if the Socialists get a new cabinet through parliament," he added.
The Socialists, now overseeing a caretaker cabinet, were given a mandate to try to form a new government on Tuesday by President Petar Stoyanov.

Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev will form the government which must be approved by the 240-seat parliament. The ruling Socialists have an absolute majority and appear determined to try to hold on to power despite 23 days of street protests.
"We may block the streets and organise human chains around the parliament," Borislavov said.
The students have avoided violence in their push for early elections but are concerned the Socialists might try to find a pretext for taking action against them.
The Socialists' youth wing plans counter-rallies on Friday and is expected to bus party faithful to Sofia to demonstrate in front of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) headquarters.
"I think the Socialists are looking for a clash but they will not get one on Friday," said Borislavov.
He said the students would respond by moving their daily rally to the Socialists' headquarters.
"We will hold our rally in front of the Socialist Party headquarters. Everyone will see who are the true Bulgarians."
